source.title: VALERIAN: Invariant Feature Learning for IMU Sensor-based Human Activity Recognition in the Wild
source.authors: Yujiao Hao; Bo-Yu Wang; Rong Zheng

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figure values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines when neural networks memorize mislabeled HAR data and reports that memorization is already non-negligible after a few epochs, qualifying the claim that clean patterns are learned first.
record.gate_note: The paper studies noisy labels in IMU activity recognition, not completely random labels in image-classification settings. Figure 4 reports training-sample categories relevant to early memorization; the plotted fractions are not stated numerically. Results cited from other papers were not extracted.
record.test_reason: Section 2.2 explicitly tests whether memorization occurs late in HAR training. Figure 4 tracks predictions on clean and mislabeled samples and reports non-negligible memorization after only a few epochs.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that subject diversity and label noise interact and can cause early memorization, undermining assumptions used by noisy-label methods. They advocate jointly handling subject differences and label noise.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes noisy-label behavior in IMU human activity recognition with DeepConvLSTM and DivideMix; it does not reproduce the original random-label image experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that early memorization is especially non-negligible under asymmetric noise. They also report that DivideMix behaves differently with single-subject and multiple-subject training data.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Internet-of-Things Design and Implementation
record.problems: The relevant Figure 4 category fractions are not given numerically in the text. Evidence is from IMU activity recognition with artificial asymmetric label noise, not random labels or image inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for V1–V5: the paper does not test those versions. Figure 3 reports DivideMix test accuracy and data partitioning, but those measures do not establish the V6 sequence of learning clean patterns before memorizing noisy labels.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels, and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect fitting of supplied training labels alongside steadily increasing test error over corruption levels from zero to complete randomization.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent fitting random labels, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.

Completely random labels and a quantitative comparison of clean-pattern and noisy-label learning rates. The single-subject comparison reports loss separation and DivideMix performance rather than direct memorization trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: V6 includes noisy labels and is not restricted to images, so this HAR experiment bears on it. Figure 10 measures accuracy against clean ground truth for label correction, rather than fitting the supplied noisy labels, and does not establish V1 or V4. The attribution of early memorization to subject diversity is the authors' interpretation; the single-subject comparison also reduces network size.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random image labels, chance test error, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time for random versus true labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily rising test error across the full range of random-label corruption.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation affect fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.

The study evaluates noisy labels in HAR, including asymmetric noise, rather than random labels; it does not directly compare learning shared real-data patterns against random-label learning over the full training trajectory.

rows.subject: DeepConvLSTM
rows.operation_detail: Tracked correct-label and wrong-label training samples by prediction category over training epochs.
rows.measure: Fractions of clean-labeled samples predicted correctly or incorrectly, and wrongly labeled samples predicted as ground truth, memorized label, or neither.
rows.value: The text states that even after a few epochs, memorization is non-negligible, especially with asymmetric noise; category fractions are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes the pattern but gives no category percentages. This is noisy-label HAR evidence, not a random-label image experiment.
rows.check: Identify the subject as DivideMix using a DeepConvLSTM backbone, rather than DeepConvLSTM alone. The value has textual support as well as a figure. Early memorization qualifies the clean-first sequence, but the supplied text does not quantify the fractions or establish that noisy labels are learned before clean patterns.
